title: When more qubits protect better
question: How did the surface-code threshold become an experimentally demonstrated quantum memory?

scope.summary: A four-paper reading path backward from the supplied 2024 surface-code memory paper. This is a selected history, not a complete error-correction survey.
scope.coverage: Four primary works from 2001–2024. Seed PDF sections I–II and the 2023 Nature results were read; the theory and primer entries use pinned abstracts. All annotations await scholarly review.
scope.search_strategy: Started from arXiv:2408.13687v1; followed its references 3, 13 and 17. Checked pinned arXiv metadata/abstracts, seed PDF, and the Nature version of record. A bounded follow-up web search found later work outside this seed-centered cutoff; it was not silently treated as covered. Checked 2026-10-17.
exclusions: A complete history of quantum error correction, including Shor, stabilizer codes and all threshold proofs.
Bosonic, ion-trap and quantum LDPC alternatives.
Later work after the selected 2024 seed cutoff.
gaps: Two entries remain abstract-grounded; no proof verification is claimed.
A memory experiment does not establish universal fault-tolerant computation or cross-device comparability.

results.label: A threshold for protection
results.summary: Surface-code recovery has a threshold: below it, increasing the code block can protect encoded information increasingly well, under explicit locality and processing assumptions.

settings.input: Topological codes on a two-dimensional qubit array.
settings.assumptions: Local gates, rapid measurements and instantaneous polynomial-size classical processing in the analyzed threshold setting.
settings.error: A threshold statement under the stated noise and recovery assumptions; no numeric threshold is extracted here.

results.label: From code to architecture
results.summary: The primer connects stabilizers, two-dimensional arrays, logical operations and resource estimates into a practical introduction to surface-code computing.

settings.input: Logical qubits encoded in a surface-code array.
settings.assumptions: Surface-code architecture and logical operations; exact resource assumptions require reading the full source.

results.label: A first scaling advantage
results.summary: A superconducting distance-5 logical memory modestly outperforms the measured distance-3 comparison. The gain depends on the device errors and decoding method.

settings.input: Superconducting surface-code memories at distances 3 and 5.
settings.assumptions: Repeated syndrome extraction; decoder and device-specific error budget.
settings.error: Logical error per cycle is measured within the experiment. This map does not rank it against a different processor.

results.label: Memory below threshold
results.summary: The seed demonstrates error suppression with code distance and a distance-7 memory, alongside a distance-5 real-time decoder. Rare correlated errors and longer computations remain distinct challenges.

settings.input: Superconducting surface-code memories at distances 3, 5 and 7.
settings.assumptions: Device-calibrated decoding and active leakage removal; memory experiments rather than universal logical computation.
settings.cost: The distance-7 memory uses 101 physical qubits including leakage removal; this is not a gate-complexity claim.
settings.error: The seed reports a distance-7 logical error per cycle of 0.143% ± 0.003%, with decoder and experimental conditions stated in section II.

relations.summary: An editorial reading connection from the threshold conditions to a surface-code introduction; not a verified theorem dependency.
The seed introduces threshold scaling with reference 3 and then measures suppression as code distance increases.
The primer provides architectural context for the memory experiment. The seed cites the later journal paper; this map inspected the earlier v1 primer and does not equate their content.
Section II explicitly follows the memory-operation methods in reference 17, the 2023 version of record. This is a method-use claim, not a cross-device bound improvement.

narrative.overview: Adding qubits can introduce more errors—or protect a logical qubit better. This reading path follows the conditions that make the second outcome possible, from a theoretical threshold to measured quantum memories.

turning_points.title: Protection has conditions
turning_points.summary: Threshold theory and surface-code constructions explain why a larger code can help, provided the physical operations and recovery procedure meet the assumptions.

turning_points.title: Test whether scaling helps
turning_points.summary: The 2022 preprint, published in 2023, finds a modest advantage when moving from distance 3 to distance 5 on the tested processor.

turning_points.title: Reach below-threshold memory
turning_points.summary: The 2024 seed demonstrates stronger distance scaling and studies real-time decoding. A reliable memory remains one component of a larger computation.
